We need homogenization for theory of polytopes, which live in affine spaces. I'd like to follow Definition 4.2 here:
https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~jean/gma-v2-root.pdf
I defined it as a type class, over arbitrary rings, and managed to prove the height 0 "axiom" from the others. However, we wonder whether this definition is general enough for everyone's needs, since we aim to get it into mathlib. For instance, we ask for the embedding to send the affine space to height 1 arbitrarily, where it could be any positive number. Are people interested in the concept in a more general setting?

import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.AffineSpace.AffineMap

namespace Affine

open Function

variable {R : Type*} [Ring R]
variable {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module R V]
variable {A : Type*} [AddTorsor V A]
variable {W : Type*} [AddCommGroup W] [Module R W]

variable (R A W) in
/-- An embedding of an affine space `A` into a vector space `W` s.t. the image of `A` is exactly the
height-1 hyperplane under a given linear height map. -/
class Homogenization extends embed : A →ᵃ[R] W where
  inj : Injective embed
  height : W →ₗ[R] R
  embed_height : embed.range = height ⁻¹' {1}
  extend (U : Type*) [AddCommGroup U] [Module R U] (f : A →ᵃ[R] U) :
    ∃! (F : W →ₗ[R] U), F ∘ embed = f
Note that that definition means that you get a different type of homogenization for every universe the type U lives in

I don't think a class is the right approach for this. Since the homogenization is unique up to isomorphism (in the right category), it's probably better to define the homogenization as a specific construction and show that it satisfies the universal property.

If this class is necessary for your use case, then it could be defined by an isomorphism with the canonical construction (similarly to docs#FreeGroupBasis). However, it's not clear what instances it would have, could you give some examples?
Also note that {embed x | (x : A)} = height ⁻¹' {1} is a very inconvenient way to write ∀ x, height (embed x) = 1
That is not equivalent, since it doesn't imply that every point with height x = 1 is in the range of embed. Also, I think that extend can be proved from the current form, avoiding the universe issue.

Attila Gáspár said:

I don't think a class is the right approach for this. Since the homogenization is unique up to isomorphism (in the right category), it's probably better to define the homogenization as a specific construction and show that it satisfies the universal property.

The class approach came out on top because we want to see homogenization as a relation between a linear space and an affine space. For example, a common use case is that we start with a linear space, choose an affine hyperplane (not containing zero), and want to consider the linear space as a homogenization of the hyperplane. There is no canonical way to go in this direction.

The canonical homogenization of an affine space (which we also implement) is one way to get a linear space from an affine space, in such a way that they are connected by this class. But even in this direction it would be rather inconvenient having to use the canonical homogenization in all cases.

Attila Gáspár said:

Also, I think that extend can be proved from the current form, avoiding the universe issue.

Yes, this should be true and it will be proven separately. Though it is not quite trivial to provide a def for this F that does not use choice.

I took a look at your branch with the homogenization. It looks like the class isn't used as a class, since you refer to the instance explicitly everywhere. So it's probably better as a normal structure.

However, there's still a disadvantage of your definition that the universal property of the homogenization cannot be implemented without choice, even for the canonical homogenizaion. So I would still recommend defining it as

structure Homogenization R A W where ofRepr ::
  repr : W ≃ₗ[R] CanonicalHomogenization R A

similarly to docs#FreeGroupBasis. I think that this would also make your use case with the homogenization of a hyperplane easier, since it is easy to construct the inverse map from CanonicalHomogenization R A, and you would only need to prove that it is bijective.

I have another remark about the definition of CanonicalHomogenization. The definition (A →ᵃ[R] R) →ₗ[R] R in your branch is likely unsuitable for Mathlib, since it works only for a finite dimensional space over a commutative ring, even though neither of these conditions is necessary. A more general implementation is to define it as a quotient of formal expressions of the form c • p + v, where c : R, p : A and v : V. What do you think about this?

Thanks for your input! This is much appreciated.
I should mention that I am supervising Olivia on this project, the code you read is written by her based on our conversations, but does not (yet) reflect everything I say here.

This would indeed work in infinite dimensions, but it still requires the commutativity of R (otherwise (A →ᵃ[R] R) is not necessarily an R-module). Unfortunately, I couldn't find a reference that considers the homogenization over a non-commutative ring, this c • p + v construction is just what I came up with when I wanted to implement the homogenization. In this construction, we identify c • p1 + v1 and c • p2 + v2iff c • (p1 -ᵥ p2) = v2 - v1.

I have implemented this construction, but I didn't make a PR because I wasn't satisfied with it. The main issue is that defining the basic operations such as addition is quite tedious because of the quotienting. I'm still not sure what the best implementation would be.

Martin Winter said:

  • I did not intend to have the instance used explicitly everywhere. I believe Olivia was trying to get rid of them, so I am not sure how much of it is actually necessary.

I'm still not convinced that this should be a class. The main issue is that to have an instance for hyperplanes, you would need to have conditions such as 0 ∉ s that cannot be automatically inferred. There's also the problem that the typeclass system assumes that instances are unique, so you cannot have multiple instances of Homogenization R A W, though this may not be a problem for hyperplanes.

Martin Winter said:

One disadvantage is that we need to forward all defs and theorems that we provide for the canonical homogenization through this structure to apply them for general homogenizations, and so we essentially need to duplicate a lot of code. No?

It does require some duplication, however, I think most properties would be easy consequences of the ones for the canonical homogenization.

Martin Winter said:

Also I don't understand why the universal property cannot be implemented without choice with our definition.

To extend a functionf : A →ᵃ[R] U to W →ₗ[R] U, you need to use f somehow, so you need to construct an element of A. But you can only construct an A if you already have an A (since neither of the functions in your Homogenization gives an A), unless you use choice.

However, the use of choice is unlikely to be a problem in this case, since the extension is unique. A reason to avoid choice is that a choice-free construction may have nice definitional equalities, but I don't think this can be reasonably achieved for the homogenization. Avoiding choice is also important if you want to do computations, but you probaly won't need computability if you are just proving general properties.

I've been thinking about the possible implementations of the canonical homogenization. I couldn't find one that is obviously better than the other ones, so I'd like to ask for opinions. Below, I assume that we have [Ring R] [Module R V] [AddTorsor V P].

Option 1: choosing an arbitrary base point

We can simply define Homogenization R P as R × V, as if P was a vector space with origin at Classical.arbitrary P. This way, the module structure on the homogenization is trivial to implement. I consider this implementation particularly inelegant due to the use of global choice, but it may be reasonable if it's not exposed.

Option 2a: quotient of formal expressions of the form c • p + v (where c : R, p : P and v : V)

This avoids the arbitrary choice, but the basic operations are more difficult to implement. Some operations, such as the embedding of V still require the use of (unique) choice.

Option 2b: quotient of formal expressions of the form c • p + v or v

The basic operations are a bit more tedious to implement compared to 2a, though the additional cases are usually trivial. This has the advantage that every operation is computable.

Option 3a: quotient of the free module ⨁ p : P, R

We get the module structure automatically, since we quotient by a submodule. Some operations are still noncomputable.

Option 3b: quotient of V × ⨁ p : P, R

The additional V is used for the embedding of V. This may make it a bit simpler to define the submodule we quotient by. It also makes it possible to implement all operations in a computable way, though we need [DecidableEq P] for that.

Option 3c: ModuleCon.Quotient of ⨁ p : P, R

This is more of a theoretical option at this point. If we ever implement an AffineSpace R P that doesn't require a vector space, then we could take the quotient by a congruence defined using affine combinations. This option would allow defining the homogenization over a semiring R. Assuming that ConvexSpace R is redefined as AffineSpace {r : R // 0 ≤ r}, this would automatically give a way of embedding a ConvexSpace into an abstract cone.

Which one of these is the most suitable for Mathlib?
What about Homogenization R p which is the homogenization with origin p : P?

I don't understand what you mean by that. There's no need to choose an origin to take the homogenization. In Option 1, the choice of origin is an implementation detail, it wouldn't be exposed in the API.

@Attila Gáspár does any subsequent theory require a unique canonical homogenisation, or can you get away with the existence of some homogenisation?
E.g. if we have

/- [...] -/

def IsHomogenization {R} [Module R W] {V} {P} W (embed : A →ᵃ[R] W) : Prop :=
  IsInjective embed ∧

  ∀ U /- ... -/, ∀ f : A →ᵃ[R] U,
    ∃! (F : W →ₗ[R] U), F ∘ embed = f

theorem has_homogenization [Nonempty P] :
    {(W, embed) | IsHomogenization R V P W embed}.Nonempty := by
  sorry /- construct every choice of `p : P` at once -/

then you may be able to parameterize theorems by
{W} [Module R W] {embed : A →ᵃ[R] W} (hW : IsHomogenization R V P W embed)
and so leave any specific choice of 'canonical' homogenisation to someone reasoning about a specific well behaved (R, V, P).

any constructed maps should then be computable (or at least not require Classical.arbitrary P)

(EDIT: IsHomogenization could also be bundled into a structure, ofc!)

My use case for the homogenization is the projective completion of an affine space, something like def ProjectiveCompletion R P := Projectivization R (Homogenization R P). I don't see a way to implement this without a canonical homogenization.

Given Module R V and AffineSpace V P we define W' := (P →ᵃ[R] R) →ₗ[R] R. This is not yet the homogenization, but almost. Let evp:W′→R,f↦f(p)\mathrm{ev_p}:W'\to R, f \mapsto f(p)evp​:W′→R,f↦f(p) be the evaluation map at p∈Pp\in Pp∈P.

The canonical homogenization W is the span of the evp,p∈P\mathrm{ev_p},p\in Pevp​,p∈P. The canonical embedding ϵ:P→W\epsilon:P\to Wϵ:P→W is given by p↦evpp\mapsto\mathrm{ev}_pp↦evp​.

The canonical linear form ω:W→R\omega:W\to Rω:W→R sends f↦f(1)f\mapsto f(\boldsymbol 1)f↦f(1), where 1\boldsymbol 11 is the constant affine map sending all points of PPP to 1. One can verify that this satisfies ω(ϵ(p))=1\omega(\epsilon(p))=1ω(ϵ(p))=1 for all p∈Pp\in Pp∈P.

The isomorphism V≃ker⁡ωV\simeq \ker \omegaV≃kerω is the map that sends v∈Vv\in Vv∈V to the map f↦f.linear(v)f\mapsto f.\mathrm{linear}(v)f↦f.linear(v). I am not sure in how far the inverse can be written down explicitly.

Given an affine form μ:P→R\mu:P\to Rμ:P→R, this extends to a linear form μ^:W→R\hat\mu:W\to Rμ^​:W→R that sends g↦g(μ)g\mapsto g(\mu)g↦g(μ). If UUU is some linear space, I think this should also give an extension of affine maps A→UA\to UA→U, which is the universal property of homogenization.
This requires the commutativity of R. I don't have a use case for the non-commutative case either, but IMO a Mathlib-quality implementation shouldn't have an unnecessary commutativity assumption.

The reason I implemented this non-constructively is that I wanted to have some design for the API first. The specific implementation could be replaced later. Which implementation we choose also depends on other factors, such as whether we add an AffineSpace over a semiring. In that case, we would probably implement Option 3c from my earlier comment. But this would mean that we can't have a computable implementation of ofVector, (unless we add a Trunc P field to AffineSpace, though this probably wouldn't work in practice, since you can't just come up with an element of an AffineSubspace).

If we don't care about affine spaces over semirings, then we could implement Option 2b, which is fully computable, at the cost of ~150 extra lines. But I imagined that Option 1 and Option 2b would have the same user-facing API, except that the internals of Option 2b wouldn't have to be hidden.

Recently we encountered a problem with the fact that Finset.affineCombination uses choice. With this homogenization this can be pervented: homogenize, do a linear combination with the same coefficients, then dehomogenize.

Small observation: if we define a ConcreteHomogenization by an isomorphism to your canonical homogenization together with suitable relations to ofPoint and weight, we run into the problem that your weight is fixed to yield value 1. If our homogenization pair is, say, a lattice over Z\Bbb ZZ and a hyperplane at height two, there is no Z\Bbb ZZ-linear form that is 1 on this hyperplane.

I am not sure anyone is going to use homogenization in such a context, but you seem to be aiming for maximal generality here, so I thought I mention it.

This is probably easy to fix by introducing a variant of weight for arbitrary values besides 1. We could then use this one instead.

The weight is just the extension of the constant 1 map, which is clearly affine even in this case. So I don't think that we can consider this a homogenization, since it doesn't satisfy the universal property.
I now tend to agree that this should not count as a homogenization.
